{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2026}}
'''Edward Eisner''' [[FRSE]] FIP (20 December 1929 – 25 December 1987) was a Hungarian-born physicist who was Professor of Applied Physics at the [[University of Strathclyde]] from 1968 to 1987.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.strath.ac.uk/media/ps/cs/gmap/academicaffairs/publications/part1201011/University_Chairs.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=7 April 2016 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304202609/http://www.strath.ac.uk/media/ps/cs/gmap/academicaffairs/publications/part1201011/University_Chairs.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> He specialised in the physics of sound.

The "Edward Eisner Memorial Fund Award" is named in his honour.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.strath.ac.uk/media/ps/cs/gmap/academicaffairs/publications/part1201011/Awards.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=7 April 2016 |archive-date=24 January 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120124164750/http://www.strath.ac.uk/media/ps/cs/gmap/academicaffairs/publications/part1201011/Awards.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Life==

Eisner was born in [[Sárvár]] in [[Hungary]] on 20 December 1929. He came to Britain with his family in the 1930s and attended the [[Belper School|Herbert Strutt School]] in [[Belper]] in [[Derbyshire]] from 1939. He won a place at [[Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge]], to study Physics and graduated BA in 1950,<ref>{{cite news |title=UNIVERSITY RESULTS: CAMBRIDGE TRIPOS LISTS |work=The Times Educational Supplement |date=23 June 1950 |page=494}}</ref> gaining a doctorate (PhD) in 1954. From 1954 he worked with the Ministry of Power at Buxton. In 1960 he went to America to work with the Bell Telephone Laboratory in [[New Jersey]], working on the improvement of handsets. In 1968 he returned to Britain to take the chair in Applied Physics at [[Strathclyde University]] retaining this role until death. He was replaced by Prof Gordon Donaldson.

In 1969 he wrote an open letter to NASA suggesting how to improve their television broadcasts from the Moon.<ref>''Glasgow Herald'' (newspaper) 27 November 1969</ref>
In 1977 he was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]]. His proposers were [[Kenneth Jack Standley]], [[Nicholas Kemmer]], Simon G G MacDonald, and [[William Cochran (physicist)|William Cochran]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Biographical Index of Former Fellows of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1783–2002|date=July 2006|publisher=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|isbn=0-902-198-84-X|url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf|access-date=7 April 2016|archive-date=24 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130124115814/http://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>
He died on Christmas Day 1987.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}
